pages.intro_copy:
Noah, Voxy and Esquire are one eight-seat van wearing three badges, sold through three different Japanese dealer networks. Australia got none of them.

This is the sensible alternative to an Alphard. Sliding doors, the same 1.8 hybrid drivetrain as a Prius, and roughly half the money.

The catch is naming. Eligibility runs off the chassis code, and the registers list this van under five different names, several of which don't say Noah or Voxy anywhere.

pages.title_tag: Toyota Porte & Spade Import Eligibility | JDM Connect
pages.intro_copy:
Almost nobody here knows this car exists, which is the entire opportunity.

Porte and Spade are the same vehicle through different Japanese dealer networks. The defining feature is one enormous sliding door on the kerb side only, with a normal hinged door for the driver.

Sounds like a gimmick until you've tried to get a kid into a car seat in a shopping centre car park, or watched someone with limited mobility get in and out of a normal car. Then it makes complete sense.

pages.h1: Is the Japanese Toyota Prius eligible for import to Australia?

faqs.a: Specific versions are. The Prius sold here, so the approvals cover the ones that did not, particularly the plug-in and the Welcab builds. Check your code and build month in the table above.
faqs.q: Is the Japanese Prius eligible for import to Australia?

faqs.a: The plug-in hybrid. Bigger battery, a plug, and enough electric range to do most short trips without the engine starting. It behaves like an EV during the week and a normal hybrid on a road trip.
A longer, taller Prius with a third row, sold only in Japan. If you want hybrid economy and seven seats in something the size of a normal car, this is close to the only answer.
Toyota's factory mobility version, with a wheelchair ramp or a lift-out passenger seat. Approved separately from the standard car, so it can be eligible when the standard one is not.
No. The Prius has been sold here for two decades and every Toyota dealer knows the hybrid system. The plug-in charging hardware is the less familiar part, so ask before you commit.

pages.title_tag: Toyota Prius JDM Import Eligibility Australia | JDM Connect
pages.intro_copy:
The Prius sold here, so importing a standard one makes no sense. What is on the register is everything Australia skipped.

The PHV is the big one, the plug-in that does real distance on battery before the engine wakes up, and it was never part of the local range in any volume. Then there are the Welcab builds with wheelchair ramps and lift-out seats, and the Prius Alpha, which is the seven seat wagon version nobody here has heard of.

ZVW52, ZVW55, MXWH61 and the Welcab entries are all separate. Read the code, not the badge.

pages.h1: Is the Toyota Supra eligible for import to Australia?

faqs.a: Depends which one and when it was built. The table above has the live register approvals. Older JZA80s may not need any of it and come in on age instead.
faqs.q: Is the Toyota Supra eligible for import to Australia?

faqs.a: Usually on age. The 25-year date rolls forward, so most A80s clear it now, and that pathway doesn't touch this register. Cars built too late for it need a live approval.
faqs.q: How do I get a JZA80 in?

faqs.a: The twin turbo is the one everyone wants and it's priced accordingly. The naturally aspirated 2JZ-GE is a lot of money less and still a good car if you want the shape rather than the timeslip. Just make sure you know which one you're buying, because plenty have been converted.

Whether it's standard, and whether the odometer and the auction sheet agree. These have been modified and traded hard for thirty years. An untouched one is worth far more than a fast one and much harder to find.
Both generations were, which is why the register windows are specific rather than open. Upside is that local knowledge and some parts already exist.

intel.watch_outs: Confirm the approval covers the exact variant (2.0 vs 3.0). BMW servicing costs apply; check for track-day use on RZ/matte editions.
intel.engine_desc: BMW-sourced 3.0 turbo six (B58) in RZ; 2.0 turbo four (B48) in SZ/SZ-R - the four was never sold in Australia.
intel.buyer_profile: Buyers wanting JDM-only grades (2.0L SZ), special editions, or manual RZs at Japanese auction pricing.
intel.why_desirable: JDM auctions offer editions and the lighter 2.0 versions Australia never received, often undercutting local A90 prices.

pages.title_tag: Toyota Supra Import Eligibility Australia | JDM Connect
pages.intro_copy:
Two Supras, thirty years apart, and the register has both.

The JZA80 is the 2JZ one. Most of them are old enough now that the register is beside the point, because they come in on age through the 25-year pathway. Check your build month before you look anywhere else, because that route is usually cheaper when it applies.

The A90 is the opposite problem. Far too young for age, and Australia sold it new, so it needs a live approval for the specific build window.
